title: 2019_PMC6668241_Identification_of_the_determinants_of_incomplete_vaccination_in_
ehr_evidence: Vaccination status was verified using the Australian Childhood Immunisation Register, a comprehensive population-based register of all childhood immunisations delivered under the National Immunisation Program (NIP).
summary: Cross-sectional survey of parents of children under 6 years attending outpatient clinics at Princess Margaret Hospital in Perth, Western Australia, examining sociodemographic and parental belief/attitude factors associated with incomplete vaccination status.
key_findings: 116 of 589 children (20%) had incomplete vaccination status.
Children with incomplete vaccination were more likely to be born overseas (OR: 3.52, 95% CI: 1.54 to 8.05).
Receiving a recommendation from a healthcare professional to delay or not complete vaccination was associated with incomplete vaccination (OR: 4.25, 95% CI: 2.07 to 8.69).
Parent non-completion of high school was associated with incomplete vaccination (OR: 2.92, 95% CI: 1.34 to 6.39) versus university-level education.
Larger family size was associated with incomplete vaccination (OR: 1.39 per one child increase, 95% CI: 1.03 to 1.87).
Parental beliefs and attitudes toward vaccination showed no significant association with incomplete vaccination after adjusting for demographic factors.
Public transport use for vaccination appointments was not significantly associated with incomplete vaccination (OR: 2.11, 95% CI: 0.78 to 5.71).
captured_features: child vaccination status (complete vs incomplete from ACIR)
use of public transport for vaccination appointments
healthcare professional recommendation to delay or not vaccinate
parental beliefs and attitudes toward vaccination (7-point Likert scale)
study_design: cross-sectional survey linked to an immunization register
population: Parents/guardians of children under 6 years (aged 2 months to 6.8 years, mean 2.4 years) attending outpatient clinics at Princess Margaret Hospital, Perth, Western Australia
exposure_domain: sociodemographic factors and parental beliefs/attitudes toward vaccination
limitations: Hospital-based sample may underrepresent high socio-economic status parents, fathers, ethnic minorities, and vaccine-refusing parents.
Survey responses were not anonymous, potentially biasing self-reported beliefs.
Cross-sectional design cannot establish causality or direction of effect.
Healthcare professional advice to delay/not vaccinate was parent-reported and not verified.
Discrepancy between parent-reported and register-recorded vaccination status may reflect incomplete overseas transfer of records.
